content: Gynecomastia is the benign enlargement of male breast glandular tissue, distinct from fat deposition (pseudogynecomastia). It is primarily caused by an imbalance between estrogens (which stimulate breast tissue growth) and androgens (which inhibit such growth), leading to proliferation of ductal and stromal elements. Gynecomastia affects men of all ages, with peaks in neonates, adolescents, and older adults. Common causes include physiological hormonal changes, medications, systemic diseases (e.g., liver or kidney failure), and endocrine disorders. Evaluation relies on thorough history, physical examination distinguishing glandular from fatty tissue, and, when indicated, laboratory tests such as hormone panels and imaging to exclude malignancy. While often benign and self-limiting, gynecomastia can cause psychosocial distress. Treatment options range from watchful waiting in reversible cases to pharmacologic therapy (e.g., selective estrogen receptor modulators) or surgical correction for persistent or severe enlargement. Safety considerations involve ruling out underlying malignancies or drug-induced causes. Synonyms include male breast enlargement, benign male breast hypertrophy, and glandular hypertrophy of the male breast. Limitations in evidence exist regarding long-term outcomes of pharmacologic treatments and optimal timing for surgery. Understanding gynecomastia is essential for appropriate management and alleviating patient concerns.

content: Gynecomastia refers to the benign enlargement of male breast glandular tissue distinguished from pseudogynecomastia, which is fatty tissue accumulation. It affects up to 65% of adolescent boys during puberty and is also prevalent among older men due to hormonal changes. Gynecomastia may be unilateral or bilateral and is classified by duration (acute versus chronic) and severity.

content: The condition results from an imbalance between estrogens, which stimulate breast tissue growth, and androgens, which counteract this effect. Increased estrogen production or sensitivity, decreased androgen levels, or peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogens can lead to ductal hyperplasia and stromal proliferation within the male breast.

content: Gynecomastia can be physiological (neonatal, pubertal, or age-related) or pathological. Pathological causes include endocrine disorders (hypogonadism, hyperthyroidism), systemic disease (liver cirrhosis, kidney failure), medications (e.g., spironolactone, cimetidine, antipsychotics), anabolic steroid use, and tumors secreting hormones. Obesity and certain herbal supplements may also contribute.

chunk_title: Physical Examination and Differentiating Gynecomastia from Pseudogynecomastia
content: Examination includes palpation of the breast to detect firm, rubbery glandular tissue concentric to the nipple distinguishing gynecomastia from soft, diffuse fatty tissue in pseudogynecomastia. Assessment includes symmetry, skin changes, lymphadenopathy, and testicular examination to rule out tumors.

content: Ultrasound is the first-line imaging for breast tissue evaluation, capable of differentiating glandular tissue from fat and identifying suspicious masses. Mammography may be used if cancer is suspected or in older men with risk factors. MRI is rarely used but informative in complex cases.

content: Physiological gynecomastia often resolves spontaneously within 6 months to 2 years. Persistent or severe gynecomastia may remain stable or progress. While benign, the condition can cause discomfort and psychological distress, necessitating treatment consideration.

chunk_title: Management Strategies: Watchful Waiting and Medical Therapy
content: Initial management in mild or recent-onset cases involves observation and addressing underlying causes. Pharmacologic options include selective estrogen receptor modulators (e.g., tamoxifen), aromatase inhibitors, and androgens, though evidence varies. Use is typically off-label and reserved for symptomatic patients.

content: Surgical intervention, such as subcutaneous mastectomy or liposuction-assisted mastectomy, is indicated for persistent, severe, or cosmetically troubling gynecomastia. Surgery effectively removes glandular tissue with good cosmetic outcomes but involves risks like scarring and altered sensation.

content: Gynecomastia can negatively affect body image, self-esteem, and mental health, particularly in adolescents and young adults. Psychological support and counseling improve coping and treatment adherence. Discussing realistic expectations is important.
